title: Ice–water interfaces drive speciation transformation and suppress bioavailability potential of freshly deposited arsenic during soil freeze–thaw cycles

Advertisement View all journals Saved research Search Account Log in Content Explore content About the journal Publish with us Subscribe Sign up for alerts RSS feed nature nature water articles article Article Published: 07 October 2026 Ice–water interfaces drive speciation transformation and suppress bioavailability potential of freshly deposited arsenic during soil freeze–thaw cycles Chen Miao 1 , 2 , Yujia Zeng 1 , 2 , Na Wu 1 , 3 , Qianhai Zhou 1 , 2 , Chaohuang Chen ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0002-2400-5693 1 , 2 , Cheng Yao 1 , 2 , Xunheng Jiang ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0001-5553-1648 1 , 2 , Yaqi Sheng 1 , 3 , Kun Yang ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-5867-7706 1 , 2 , Daohui Lin ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-9662-7195 1 , 2 , Lizhong Zhu 1 , 2 & … Jiang Xu ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-0369-4848 1 , 2 , 4 Show authors Nature Water ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research 62 Accesses Metrics details Abstract Ubiquitous freeze–thaw cycles serve as a hidden driver reshaping arsenic (As) bioavailability in industrial and adjacent agricultural soils impacted by industrial emissions. Here we show that ice–water interfaces trigger rapid changes in the speciation and bioavailability potential of freshly deposited As particles in soils, primarily within the first three freeze–thaw cycles. Many industrial parks and nearby farmlands are located in regions with subzero temperatures that coincide with or follow precipitation, frequently inducing freeze–thaw events. These conditions reduced the As relative leachability ratio (unfrozen before) by an average of 71% in 50 diverse soil samples from across China. Quasi-in situ and single-particle analysis unveiled As transformations into relatively stable forms (for example, ferric arsenate and haematite-associated As) during freeze–thaw cycles. Beyond typical environmental factors, concentration effects induced fluctuations in chemistry in the microenvironment of ice boundaries that steered speciation changes, while physical fragmentation redistributed As mass across particle-size fractions. This study reveals the previously overlooked role of natural freeze–thaw dynamics in altering the speciation and reactivity of freshly deposited heavy metal particles in cold and wet conditions, providing new insights into their initial geochemical fate following industrial emission.
